newsitem.title: USA: Environmentalists split on climate change plan.
newsitem.headline: Environmentalists split on climate change plan.

text.p: In its effort to get an international agreement to fight global warming, the Clinton administration faces opposition not only from polluting industries, but from a fractious environmental community.

Some environmentalists accused the administration of caving to industries' demands or taking the path of least political resistance with the plan it offered last week to use market incentives to spur countries to reduce pollution from burning fossil fuels.

Other environmentalists say such a plan, which relies more on carrots than sticks, is the only way to get countries to cooperate to stop climate change caused by the accumulation of heat-trapping gases in the atmosphere.

"I think the environmental community agrees that 1 degree Celsius (1.7 degree Fahrenheit) warming over the next century is the most we can sustain and that cuts (of pollution) have to start in 2005. It's just the mechanism for getting there," Ann Mesnikoff, of the Sierra Club's Global Warming and Energy Program, said.

In papers for international negotations, the administration proposed setting legally binding limits on industrialized countries' emissions, although it has not yet suggested a numerical target for emissions cuts.
Countries that pollute below the cap could sell the difference to other countries as emissions credits.
The United States has used this kind of plan to reduce emissions from coal-burning power plants. Credits, or pollution permits, are traded at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Backers of this kind of scheme say it will provide the most cost-efficient means of reducing pollution, and give countries flexibility in reaching their targets.
Countries able to reduce emissions at relatively low cost could sell credits to countries that face higher costs.
The administration also proposed letting countries "bank" their pollution credits to use later, or to borrow against future emissions reductions if they pay a penalty.
It also wants industrialized countries, operating under legally binding emissions caps, to be able to use projects in developing countries to meet their targets.

For example, with this plan an industrialized country could sell technology for a cleaner power plant to a developing country and get credit for pollution reductions from the plant that would have been built otherwise.

The Environmental Defense Fund supports the trading approach, saying it will encourage technological innovations, bring developing countries into the climate change agreement and be the most enforceable scheme on the international level.
They also say emissions trading is a preferrable option to imposing international energy taxes, or requiring specific types of pollution controls or energy efficiency standards.
But other groups including the Sierra Club and Greenpeace oppose the plan, saying it will create a kind of shell game in which pollution may be shifted but not reduced.
"People perceive trading as the one key you can push and it will make all the reductions happen without taking a stand on the hard issues," Mesnikoff, of the Sierra Club, said.
Instead, she said, countries should take tough actions to reduce pollution, such as requiring higher automobile fuel efficiency or switching power plants from coal to natural gas.
The Natural Resources Defense Council supports emissions trading, but said the plan needs tighter enforcement rules.
"The risk is you have some rogue country that sells a lot of allowances, then is out of compliance at the end," Dan Lashof, an NRDC senior scientist, said.

The NRDC and many other groups also oppose gaining credits from projects with developing countries, saying emissions reductions cannot be measured from "what would have happened" without the industrialized nation's participation.

The Global Climate Coalition of U.S. industries that oppose tougher pollution controls said the administration should not push such schemes until it has analyzed potential economic impacts on the United States. It also wants developing countries, where emissions are increasing, to have more responsibilities to cut pollution.

"It raises a lot of questions in terms of impacts and what will it cost the U.S., how does it affect our competitiveness, how do you monitor and develop a method of compliance," John Shlaes, executive director of the coalition, said.
